groups.name: Rhythm
groups.blurb: What the atria and ventricles are doing, and whether the two are still talking to each other.

groups.name: Conduction
groups.blurb: Where the impulse is delayed or blocked on its way down.

groups.name: Chamber enlargement
groups.blurb: Voltage and morphology changes that follow a chamber working against a load.

groups.name: Ischemia and infarction
groups.blurb: ST-T and Q wave patterns, grouped by the territory they point at.

groups.name: Other patterns
groups.blurb: Repolarization, drug effect, and the normal tracing you compare everything against.

categories.name: Normal ECG
categories.teaching: The reference tracing. Sinus rhythm, PR 120 to 200 ms, QRS under 120 ms, no pathologic Q waves, concordant T waves, and an axis between -30 and +90 degrees. Reading abnormal tracings well depends on having a large internal library of normal ones, which is the least glamorous and most useful thing on this page.

categories.name: Sinus tachycardia
categories.teaching: Rate above 100 with a P wave before every QRS and a QRS after every P. The morphology is normal; the rate is the finding. Sinus tachycardia is almost always a response to something else, so the diagnostic work is naming that something rather than treating the rate.

categories.name: Sinus bradycardia
categories.teaching: Rate below 60 with normal sinus morphology and conduction. Common and benign in trained athletes and during sleep. It matters when it is symptomatic, when it is drug induced, or when it appears alongside conduction disease that suggests the whole system is failing rather than the node alone.

categories.name: Sinus arrhythmia
categories.teaching: Sinus rhythm with beat to beat variation in the R-R interval, classically phasic with respiration. P wave morphology stays constant, which is what separates it from a wandering atrial pacemaker. A normal finding, and its absence in a young patient is the more interesting observation.

categories.name: Atrial fibrillation
categories.teaching: Irregularly irregular ventricular response with no organized P waves, replaced by a fibrillatory baseline best seen in V1. The irregularity is the diagnosis; rate can be anything. Look at a long rhythm strip rather than a 2.5 second window, because irregularity is a property of a sequence.

categories.name: Atrial flutter
categories.teaching: Organized atrial activity near 300 per minute producing sawtooth flutter waves, best seen in the inferior leads and V1. Conduction is usually 2 to 1, which parks the ventricular rate near 150 and is why a regular rate of exactly 150 should always prompt a hunt for flutter waves.

categories.name: Supraventricular tachycardia
categories.teaching: Regular narrow complex tachycardia, typically 150 to 250, with P waves absent, buried in the QRS, or retrograde. Narrow means the ventricles are being activated through the normal system, which places the circuit at or above the AV node.

codes.label: low QRS voltages in the frontal and horizontal leads

categories.name: Ventricular premature complexes
categories.teaching: Early, wide, bizarre QRS complexes with no preceding P wave and discordant T waves, usually followed by a full compensatory pause. Uniform morphology suggests a single focus. The finding is usually benign in a structurally normal heart, and the tracing cannot tell you whether the heart is structurally normal.

categories.name: Bigeminy
categories.description: bigeminal pattern (unknown origin, SV or Ventricular)
categories.teaching: Every sinus beat followed by a premature complex, producing a repeating couplet. The pattern is the point: grouped beating is a clue to look for a fixed relationship rather than random ectopy. PTB-XL does not specify supraventricular versus ventricular origin for this label.

categories.name: Paced rhythm
categories.teaching: Pacing spikes preceding the complex they capture. Ventricular pacing produces a wide QRS, usually with a left bundle branch pattern from a right ventricular lead. A paced ventricular rhythm obscures the underlying repolarization, which is why the usual ischemia criteria do not apply.

categories.name: First degree AV block
categories.teaching: PR interval above 200 ms with every P conducted. Not truly a block but a uniform delay, most often in the AV node. Isolated and asymptomatic it needs nothing; combined with bifascicular block it becomes part of a more worrying picture.

categories.name: Second degree AV block
categories.teaching: Some P waves conduct and some do not. Mobitz I shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat and usually sits in the node. Mobitz II drops beats without warning and sits below it, which is why Mobitz II is the one that earns a pacemaker.

categories.name: Third degree AV block
categories.teaching: Complete AV dissociation: regular P waves and a regular escape rhythm, marching independently, with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular. The escape QRS width tells you the level of the block, and a narrow junctional escape is considerably more stable than a wide ventricular one.

categories.name: Complete right bundle branch block
categories.teaching: QRS at or above 120 ms with an rSR' in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in I and V6. The right ventricle is depolarized late and through muscle rather than conducting tissue. Appropriate discordance means the T wave in the right precordial leads points away from the terminal QRS.

categories.name: Incomplete right bundle branch block
categories.teaching: The right bundle pattern with a QRS under 120 ms. Common, often nothing. Worth a second look when it appears with right axis deviation or right atrial enlargement, where it may be reporting right ventricular volume load rather than conduction disease.

categories.name: Complete left bundle branch block
categories.teaching: QRS at or above 120 ms with a broad monophasic R in I, aVL and V6, and a dominant S in V1. Left bundle branch block reverses the direction of septal depolarization and rewrites repolarization wholesale, so ordinary ST criteria fail and the Sgarbossa criteria exist to work around it.

categories.name: Left anterior fascicular block
categories.teaching: Left axis deviation beyond -45 degrees with qR in aVL, rS inferiorly, and a normal or near normal QRS duration. The commonest conduction abnormality on any ECG collection. Alone it means little; with right bundle branch block it is bifascicular block.

codes.label: low QRS voltages in the frontal and horizontal leads

categories.name: Left posterior fascicular block
categories.teaching: Right axis deviation with rS in I and aVL and qR inferiorly, once other causes of right axis have been excluded. The posterior fascicle is short, thick and dual supplied, so isolated posterior fascicular block is genuinely rare and the diagnosis is one of exclusion.

categories.name: Nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay
categories.teaching: QRS at or above 120 ms without meeting criteria for either bundle branch pattern. A description rather than a diagnosis. Causes include hyperkalemia, sodium channel blockade, cardiomyopathy and prior infarction, so it is a prompt to look outside the tracing.

categories.name: Ventricular pre-excitation
categories.teaching: Short PR, a delta wave slurring the QRS upstroke, and a widened QRS from fusion between the accessory pathway and the normal system. Secondary ST-T changes follow the abnormal depolarization and should not be read as ischemia. Pre-excitation with atrial fibrillation is the dangerous combination, because the pathway can conduct rapidly without the AV node's protective delay.

categories.name: Left ventricular hypertrophy
categories.teaching: Increased QRS voltage by any of several criteria, commonly S in V1 plus R in V5 or V6 above 35 mm, with a strain pattern of downsloping ST depression and T inversion in the lateral leads. Voltage criteria are specific and quite insensitive, and body habitus moves them considerably.

categories.name: Right ventricular hypertrophy
categories.teaching: Right axis deviation with a dominant R in V1, deep S waves laterally, and often right atrial enlargement and repolarization change in the right precordial leads. Insensitive, so a normal tracing does not exclude it.

categories.name: Left atrial enlargement
categories.teaching: A broad notched P in the limb leads with a wide, deep terminal negative component in V1. Reflects delayed left atrial activation. Common wherever left sided filling pressures are chronically raised, most often mitral valve disease and diastolic dysfunction.

categories.name: Right atrial enlargement
categories.teaching: A tall peaked P wave, classically at or above 2.5 mm in the inferior leads, with a prominent initial positive component in V1. Reflects increased right atrial mass or pressure and travels with pulmonary disease, pulmonary hypertension and tricuspid disease.

categories.name: Inferior myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Q waves and T wave changes in II, III and aVF. Usually a right coronary territory event. Reciprocal change in I and aVL supports it, and inferior involvement should always prompt right sided leads to look for right ventricular infarction.

categories.name: Anteroseptal myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Q waves and loss of R wave progression in V1 to V3 or V4, a left anterior descending territory pattern. Poor R wave progression alone is nonspecific and is produced just as easily by lead placement, body habitus and left ventricular hypertrophy.

codes.label: low QRS voltages in the frontal and horizontal leads

categories.name: Anterolateral myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Q waves and T wave change spanning the anterior and lateral leads, V4 through V6 with I and aVL. Implies a proximal left anterior descending or a large diagonal territory, and therefore a larger amount of myocardium than a septal pattern.

categories.name: Inferolateral myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Inferior and lateral involvement together, II, III and aVF with V5, V6, I and aVL. Fits a dominant right coronary artery or a left circumflex territory depending on coronary anatomy.

categories.name: Nonspecific ischemic ST-T change
categories.teaching: ST depression or T wave inversion that does not localize to a single territory. The label is honest about its own uncertainty. It carries weight with symptoms and prior tracings, and very little without either.

categories.name: Subendocardial injury, anteroseptal
categories.teaching: Horizontal or downsloping ST depression across the anteroseptal leads, the pattern of demand ischemia or subendocardial injury rather than transmural infarction. Widespread ST depression with elevation in aVR raises the question of left main or proximal multivessel disease.

categories.name: Long QT interval
categories.teaching: A prolonged rate corrected QT, conventionally above 460 ms in women and 450 ms in men. Measure in the lead with the clearest T wave offset and beware of merging a U wave into the measurement. Matters because it is the substrate for torsades de pointes, and because the common causes are drugs and electrolytes, both of which are fixable.

categories.name: Digitalis effect
categories.teaching: Downsloping scooped ST depression, the so called reverse tick, with a shortened QT and flattened T waves. This is the ECG signature of a therapeutic digoxin level, not of toxicity. Digoxin toxicity is an arrhythmic diagnosis, most characteristically atrial tachycardia with block.

codes.label: voltage criteria (QRS) for left ventricular hypertrophy

categories.name: Atrial premature complexes
categories.teaching: An early P wave of different morphology from the sinus P, conducting to a normal narrow QRS, usually followed by an incomplete compensatory pause. A very early atrial beat can find the bundle refractory and conduct with aberrancy, which is the commonest reason a supraventricular beat looks ventricular.

categories.name: Trigeminy
categories.description: trigeminal pattern (unknown origin, SV or Ventricular)
categories.teaching: Every third beat is premature, producing repeating groups of three. Like bigeminy this is a pattern of coupling rather than a diagnosis, and the useful observation is that the ectopy is organized rather than random.

categories.name: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia
categories.teaching: An abrupt onset and offset regular narrow complex tachycardia, most often AV nodal reentry. The abruptness is what distinguishes it from sinus tachycardia, which accelerates and decelerates gradually. Retrograde P waves may appear as a pseudo r' in V1 or a pseudo S in the inferior leads.

categories.name: Supraventricular arrhythmia
categories.teaching: Irregular supraventricular activity that does not meet criteria for fibrillation or flutter. Multifocal atrial tachycardia sits here when three or more P wave morphologies are present, a pattern that travels with severe pulmonary disease.

categories.name: Incomplete left bundle branch block
categories.teaching: A left bundle pattern with a QRS between 100 and 120 ms. Loss of the normal septal q wave in the lateral leads is the early sign. Less benign than its right sided counterpart, since left sided conduction disease more often reflects underlying structural heart disease.

categories.name: Pathologic Q waves
categories.teaching: Q waves at or above 40 ms wide, or deeper than a quarter of the following R wave, in a contiguous territory. They indicate established myocardial loss rather than acute injury, and they persist. Normal septal q waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6 are narrow and shallow and mean nothing.

codes.label: voltage criteria (QRS) for left ventricular hypertrophy

categories.name: Abnormal QRS
categories.teaching: QRS morphology outside normal limits without meeting criteria for a specific block or infarct pattern. Poor R wave progression, fragmentation and abnormal initial forces live here. A descriptive label that earns meaning only next to a prior tracing or a clinical question.

categories.name: ST depression
categories.teaching: ST segment depression measured at the J point relative to the TP baseline. Horizontal and downsloping depression carries far more weight than upsloping. Diffuse depression with elevation in aVR suggests global subendocardial ischemia rather than a single territory.

categories.name: ST elevation
categories.teaching: ST elevation in contiguous leads. The differential is wider than occlusion: pericarditis, early repolarization, left ventricular aneurysm, Brugada, hyperkalemia and left bundle branch block all produce it. Reciprocal depression is the finding that most favors occlusion.

categories.name: T wave inversion
categories.teaching: Inverted T waves outside the leads where inversion is normal, being III, aVR and V1. Deep symmetric inversion across the anterior leads raises the question of critical proximal left anterior descending stenosis. T inversion is also the expected secondary change wherever depolarization is abnormal, so it means much less inside a bundle branch block.

categories.name: Nonspecific ST change
categories.teaching: Minor ST segment change that does not meet threshold criteria and does not localize. Extremely common and, on its own, close to uninterpretable. Its value is comparative: the same tracing next to a prior one is either reassuring or not.

categories.name: Non-diagnostic T abnormality
categories.teaching: T wave flattening or minor inversion falling short of a diagnostic pattern. One of the most frequent statements in any ECG collection, and one of the least actionable. It is included here precisely so the pattern is recognizable as background rather than signal.

categories.name: Anterior myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Q waves and R wave loss across the anterior precordial leads. A left anterior descending territory pattern. Large anterior infarction is the classic substrate for ventricular aneurysm, which is worth remembering when persistent ST elevation appears months later.

categories.name: Lateral myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Q waves and T change in I, aVL, V5 and V6, a circumflex or diagonal territory. Isolated lateral infarction is uncommon and easy to miss, because the high lateral leads get less attention than the anterior and inferior groups.

categories.name: Inferoposterior myocardial infarction
categories.teaching: Inferior changes with posterior extension: a tall R and ST depression in V1 to V3 that mirrors posterior injury seen from the front. Posterior leads V7 to V9 convert the mirror image into direct evidence and should be obtained when this pattern appears.

categories.name: Ischemia, anterolateral leads
categories.teaching: Ischemic ST-T change localized to the anterolateral leads. Territory localization on the surface ECG is a reasonable guide to the culprit vessel and a poor one to the extent of disease.

categories.name: Ischemia, inferior leads
categories.teaching: Ischemic ST-T change in II, III and aVF. Right coronary territory in most people, left circumflex in those with a dominant circumflex.

categories.name: Ischemia, anteroseptal leads
categories.teaching: Ischemic change across V1 to V3 or V4. Septal leads are also the ones most affected by electrode placement, so confirm the tracing before committing to a territory.

categories.name: Ischemia, lateral leads
categories.teaching: Ischemic change in I, aVL, V5 and V6. The high lateral leads I and aVL are also where reciprocal change from an inferior event appears, so read them together with the inferior group.

categories.name: Subendocardial injury, anterolateral
categories.teaching: ST depression across the anterolateral leads, the demand ischemia pattern rather than transmural injury. Common in tachycardia, anemia and hypotension without any acute plaque event.

categories.name: Low voltage
categories.description: low QRS voltages in the frontal and horizontal leads
categories.teaching: QRS amplitude under 5 mm in all limb leads or under 10 mm in all precordial leads. The differential is anything that puts material between heart and electrode or reduces muscle: pericardial effusion, obesity, emphysema, infiltrative disease and severe hypothyroidism.

categories.name: High voltage
categories.teaching: QRS amplitude above normal limits without the full hypertrophy pattern. Very common in thin young people, where it means nothing. Voltage criteria are a poor test in isolation and this category is here to demonstrate that.

categories.name: Septal hypertrophy
categories.teaching: Prominent septal forces, classically deep narrow Q waves in the lateral and inferior leads with high voltage. Worth recognizing because it can imitate infarction while pointing instead at hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

categories.name: Ventricular aneurysm pattern
categories.description: ST-T changes compatible with ventricular aneurysm
categories.teaching: Persistent ST elevation with Q waves in a territory weeks or months after infarction. The finding that separates it from acute injury is time: elevation that has not evolved. Usually anterior and usually accompanied by a large prior infarct.

categories.name: Electrolyte disturbance or drug effect
categories.teaching: Repolarization change attributable to electrolytes or medication. Peaked T waves and QRS widening with hyperkalemia, U waves and a long QU with hypokalemia, a short QT with hypercalcemia. The ECG is faster than the chemistry panel, which is the entire reason to look.
